records.source: Ἀλήθειαν λέγω ἐν Χριστῷ, οὐ ψεύδομαι, συμμαρτυρούσης μοι τῆς συνειδήσεώς μου ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, ὅτι λύπη μοί ἐστιν μεγάλη καὶ ἀδιάλειπτος ὀδύνη τῇ καρδίᾳ μου·
records.gloss: Truth I speak in Christ, not I lie, bearing witness with me the conscience of me in [the] Spirit Holy, \v 2 that grief to me is great and unceasing anguish in the heart of me;
pieces: I am telling the truth in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}; I am not lying. My conscience, in the Holy Spirit, bears witness with me
that my sorrow is great and the pain in my heart never stops.

L.1: I speak [the] truth in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, I am not lying, my conscience bearing witness with me in [the] Holy Spirit,
L.2: that I have great grief and unceasing anguish in my heart.

R.1: I belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, and I am telling you the truth. I am not lying. My conscience agrees with what I say, and the Holy Spirit guides my conscience.
R.2: I am very sad, and my heart hurts all the time.

decisions.choice: in Christ: speaking as one who belongs to Christ
decisions.reason: Paul speaks as a man joined to Christ and answerable to him, so his words can be trusted. He says the same in 2 Corinthians 2:17 and 12:19.

decisions.choice: his conscience is a second witness, and the Holy Spirit stands behind it
alternatives: "in the Holy Spirit" goes with "I speak"
decisions.reason: The participle συμμαρτυρούσης means "bearing witness together with". Paul's own word and his conscience make two witnesses (compare Deuteronomy 19:15). "In the Holy Spirit" most likely goes with the conscience: the Spirit confirms what it says, as in 8:16.

decisions.choice: the cause of his grief is left unsaid until verse 3
decisions.reason: Paul states his grief before he names its cause: most of his own people, Israel, have not believed in the Messiah (verses 3-5, 30-32; 10:1).

decisions.choice: I belong to Christ; the Holy Spirit guides my conscience
decisions.reason: Readable turns "in Christ" and "in the Holy Spirit" into short sentences, as the meaning decisions explain them.

records.heading: Paul's grief for Israel

records.source: ηὐχόμην γὰρ ἀνάθεμα εἶναι αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν συγγενῶν μου κατὰ σάρκα, οἵτινές εἰσιν Ἰσραηλῖται, ὧν ἡ υἱοθεσία καὶ ἡ δόξα καὶ αἱ διαθῆκαι καὶ ἡ νομοθεσία καὶ ἡ λατρεία καὶ αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι, ὧν οἱ πατέρες, καὶ ἐξ ὧν ὁ χριστὸς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων, θεὸς εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας· ἀμήν.
records.gloss: For was wishing accursed to be myself I from the Christ on behalf of the brothers of me, the kinsmen of me according to flesh, \v 4 who are Israelites, of whom the adoption and the glory and the covenants and the lawgiving and the worship and the promises, \v 5 of whom the fathers, and from whom the Christ, the [part] according to flesh, the [one] being over all, God blessed to the ages; amen.
pieces: I could even wish that I myself were under a curse, cut off from {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, on behalf of my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, my own people by human descent.
They are Israelites. Theirs is the adoption as God's children, theirs the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship and the promises.
The patriarchs are theirs, and from them, by human descent, comes {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

L.3: For I could wish that I myself were accursed [and cut off] from the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} for the sake of my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, my kinsfolk according to [the] flesh,
L.4: who are Israelites, to whom [belong] the adoption and the glory and the covenants and the giving of the law and the worship and the promises,
L.5: to whom [belong] the fathers, and from whom [is] the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed to the ages. Amen.

R.3: I would even be willing to be cursed and cut off from {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, if that could help my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, my own people by birth.
R.4: They are the people of Israel. God adopted them as {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} children and showed them {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory. He made covenants with them and gave them the law. He showed them how to worship {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave them {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} promises.
R.5: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were their ancestors. And as a human being, {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} came from their people. He is God over all things, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is to be praised forever. Amen.

decisions.choice: accursed: handed over to God's judgment and cut off from Christ
decisions.reason: ἀνάθεμα is something devoted to God for destruction (Joshua 6:17, 7:1), and so a person under God's curse (1 Corinthians 16:22, Galatians 1:8-9). "From Christ" says what the curse would mean for Paul: being cut off from him.

decisions.choice: a wish he cannot carry out
decisions.reason: The imperfect ηὐχόμην expresses a wish that cannot or will not come true: "I could wish". Paul echoes Moses, who asked to be blotted out of God's book if Israel could not be forgiven (Exodus 32:32). Romans 8:38-39 has just said nothing can separate him from Christ.

decisions.choice: according to the flesh: by physical descent
decisions.reason: σάρξ here is human birth and family line, not the sinful self: the Jews are Paul's people by birth, and the Messiah is from Israel as a human being, as in 1:3.

decisions.choice: the adoption: Israel made God's son
decisions.reason: God called Israel "my firstborn son" (Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1). Paul has used the same word for believers in 8:15 and 8:23.

decisions.choice: the glory: God's glorious presence among Israel
decisions.reason: The glory is God's presence shown to Israel at Sinai, in the tabernacle and in the temple (Exodus 24:16-17, 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10-11).

decisions.choice: the worship: the worship God gave Israel in the tabernacle and temple
decisions.reason: λατρεία is service offered to God, here the priesthood, sacrifices and festivals of the law (Hebrews 9:1, 9:6). Paul uses it for the worship of believers in 12:1.

decisions.choice: Christ "who is God over all, blessed forever": the words describe the Messiah
alternatives: a full stop after "according to the flesh": "May God, who is over all, be blessed forever"
a stop after "over all": "the Messiah, who is over all. God be blessed forever"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates with a comma after "according to the flesh", so that "who is over all, God blessed forever" describes the Messiah. In favor: the words "who is" most naturally refer back to the person just named; "according to the flesh" leads one to expect what he is beyond his human descent; and a separate blessing of God normally puts "blessed" first ("Blessed be God", 2 Corinthians 1:3), while here it follows the one just named, as in 1:25 and 2 Corinthians 11:31. Against: Paul nowhere else plainly calls Christ "God", and some manuscripts and readers put a full stop after "flesh", making the rest a separate praise: "God who is over all be blessed forever." The oldest manuscripts have no punctuation, so the choice is made from the sense.

decisions.choice: by human descent (B); by birth, as a human being (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "according to the flesh" means here, as Romans 1:3 does.

decisions.choice: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
decisions.reason: Readable names "the fathers": the patriarchs with whom God made his promises (Exodus 3:15).

decisions.choice: God adopted them; showed them his glory; made covenants; gave them the law; showed them how to worship
decisions.reason: Readable turns the list of nouns into sentences that say what God did for Israel, following the meaning decisions.

records.source: Οὐχ οἷον δὲ ὅτι ἐκπέπτωκεν ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Not such however as that has fallen the word of the God.
pieces: But this does not mean that God's word has failed.

L.6: But [it is] not as though the word of God has failed.

R.6: But this does not mean that God has failed to keep {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} promises.

decisions.choice: the word of God: God's promises to Israel
decisions.reason: Paul has just listed the promises (verse 4), and verse 9 calls God's word to Abraham "a word of promise". The question is whether Israel's unbelief means those promises have come to nothing.

decisions.choice: has failed: has fallen short of its purpose
decisions.reason: ἐκπίπτω is to fall, and so to fail or come to nothing (compare 1 Corinthians 13:8).

decisions.choice: failed to keep his promises
decisions.reason: Readable says what "the word of God" refers to here.

records.heading: God's word has not failed

records.source: οὐ γὰρ πάντες οἱ ἐξ Ἰσραήλ, οὗτοι Ἰσραήλ·
records.gloss: Not for all the [ones] from Israel, these [are] Israel;
pieces: For not everyone descended from Israel truly belongs to Israel.

L.6: For not all who [are] from Israel, these [are] Israel;

R.6: Not everyone who is born into the family of Israel is part of the true Israel, God's people.

decisions.choice: two senses of Israel: the people descended from Jacob, and the people of God's promise within it
alternatives: the second "Israel" is the church of Jews and Gentiles
decisions.reason: The first "Israel" is the nation by descent from Jacob, whose other name was Israel (Genesis 32:28). The second is the people God has chosen and called, who are not simply the same as the nation (verses 7-13; compare 2:28-29 and 11:5). Here Paul is still speaking of Israel; he is not calling Gentile believers "Israel".

decisions.choice: truly belongs to (B); the true Israel, God's people (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the repeated "Israel" means, following the meaning decision.

records.source: οὐδ’ ὅτι εἰσὶν σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ, πάντες τέκνα, ἀλλ’· Ἐν Ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα.
records.gloss: Nor because they are seed of Abraham [are they] all children, but: In Isaac will be called to you seed.
pieces: Nor are they all Abraham's children just because they are his descendants. Rather, "It is through Isaac that your offspring will be named."

L.7: Nor, because they are Abraham's seed, [are they] all [his] children, but: "Through Isaac your seed will be named."

R.7: And not all of Abraham's descendants are truly his children. God told Abraham, "Your family line will be counted through Isaac."

decisions.choice: Genesis 21:12
decisions.reason: God says this to Abraham when Sarah wants Hagar and Ishmael sent away: Abraham's promised line will come through Isaac, not through Ishmael, though both were his sons. Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament word for word.

decisions.choice: will be named: will be reckoned as your offspring
decisions.reason: καλέω is "call" or "name". In Genesis it means that Isaac's line will count as Abraham's offspring. Paul goes on to use the same verb for God's calling (verses 12, 24-26).

decisions.choice: God told Abraham
decisions.reason: Readable says who spoke the words of the quotation and to whom (Genesis 21:12).

records.source: τοῦτ’ ἔστιν, οὐ τὰ τέκνα τῆς σαρκὸς ταῦτα τέκνα τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας λογίζεται εἰς σπέρμα·
records.gloss: That is, not the children of the flesh, these [are] children of the God, but the children of the promise are counted for seed;
pieces: This means that it is not the children born by natural descent who are God's children. It is the children of the promise who are counted as Abraham's offspring.

L.8: That is, [it is] not the children of the flesh [who are] children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed.

R.8: This means that being born into Abraham's family does not make anyone a child of God. The children born because of God's promise are the ones counted as Abraham's true family.

decisions.choice: children of the flesh: children by natural birth only
decisions.reason: σάρξ here is ordinary human descent, as with Ishmael, who was "born according to the flesh" (Galatians 4:23), in contrast to Isaac, born by God's promise.

decisions.choice: children of the promise: those born because of what God promised
decisions.reason: Isaac was born because God promised him to Abraham and Sarah when they were too old to have children (4:18-21, Genesis 18:10-14). Paul makes him the pattern for all whom God counts as Abraham's offspring (Galatians 4:28).

decisions.choice: are counted: are reckoned by God
decisions.reason: λογίζομαι is the verb Paul used in chapter 4 for faith being counted as righteousness (4:3-5). God himself decides who are counted as Abraham's offspring.

decisions.choice: Abraham's offspring (B); Abraham's true family (R)
decisions.reason: The offspring are Abraham's, as in verse 7; Balanced and Readable say so.

decisions.choice: by natural descent
decisions.reason: Balanced says what "of the flesh" means here; it is not the sinful self of 8:3-9.

records.source: ἐπαγγελίας γὰρ ὁ λόγος οὗτος· Κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦτον ἐλεύσομαι καὶ ἔσται τῇ Σάρρᾳ υἱός.
records.gloss: Of promise for the word this [is]: At the time this I will come and there will be to the Sarah a son.
pieces: For this is what the promise said: "At this time I will come back, and a son will be born to Sarah."

L.9: For this word [is a word] of promise: "At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son."

R.9: This is the promise God made: "At this time next year I will come back, and Sarah will have a son."

decisions.choice: Genesis 18:10 and 18:14
decisions.reason: God promised Abraham at Mamre that Sarah, old and without children, would have a son "at the set time", that is, about a year later. Paul combines the wording of the two verses in their Greek form. In the Hebrew of 18:14 the speaker is named with the divine name.

decisions.choice: the emphasis falls on "promise"
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "of promise" first: this word was a promise, so Isaac was a child of the promise (verse 8), not merely of natural birth.

decisions.choice: At this time next year
decisions.reason: In Genesis 18:10 and 18:14 "this time" means the same season a year later; Readable says so.

records.source: οὐ μόνον δέ, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ῥεβέκκα ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα, Ἰσαὰκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν·
records.gloss: Not only and, but also Rebecca, from one conception having, Isaac the father of us;
pieces: And that is not all. Rebecca also conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac.

L.10: And not only [that], but also Rebecca, having conceived by one [man], Isaac our father;

R.10: Here is another example. Rebecca became pregnant with twins, and both had the same father, our ancestor Isaac.

decisions.choice: an unfinished sentence, taken up again in verses 11-12
decisions.reason: The Greek has no main verb: Paul begins with Rebecca, breaks off to explain (verse 11), and finishes with "it was said to her" (verse 12). A verb such as "conceived" or "had children" is understood.

decisions.choice: conceived by one man: both sons had the same father and the same conception
decisions.reason: κοίτη means a bed, and so conception. The point is that Jacob and Esau were twins, with the same father and mother (Genesis 25:21-24), unlike Ishmael and Isaac. Descent made no difference between them.

decisions.choice: our father Isaac: ancestor of Israel, and of all who believe
decisions.reason: Isaac is "our father" because Paul is a Jew; he has also called Abraham the father of all who believe (4:11-12, 4:16).

decisions.choice: pregnant with twins
decisions.reason: Readable says what "conceived by one man" points to, from Genesis 25:24.

records.source: μήπω γὰρ γεννηθέντων μηδὲ πραξάντων τι ἀγαθὸν ἢ φαῦλον, ἵνα ἡ κατ’ ἐκλογὴν πρόθεσις τοῦ θεοῦ μένῃ, οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἀλλ’ ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος, ἐρρέθη αὐτῇ ὅτι Ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι·
records.gloss: For not yet having been born nor having done anything good or bad, so that the according to election purpose of the God might remain, \v 12 not from works but from the [one] calling, it was said to her that: The greater will serve the lesser;
pieces: The children were not yet born and had done nothing good or bad. Yet so that God's purpose in choosing might stand,
a purpose that rests not on works but on the one who calls, Rebecca was told, "The older will serve the younger."

L.11: For [when they had] not yet been born nor done anything good or bad, so that the purpose of God according to election might stand,
L.12: not from works but from the [one] who calls, it was said to her, "The older will serve the younger."

R.11: Her sons had not yet been born. They had not done anything good or bad. God made {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} choice then, so that {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} plan would stand firm.
R.12: It depends on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} call, not on what people do. So God told Rebecca, "The older son will serve the younger one."

decisions.choice: Genesis 25:23
decisions.reason: God told Rebecca, while the twins struggled within her, that two nations were in her womb and that the older would serve the younger. Paul quotes the last line of the oracle as it stands in the Greek Old Testament.

decisions.choice: God's purpose according to election: his plan, carried out by his choosing
alternatives: God's purpose of foreseeing who would choose him
decisions.reason: ἐκλογή is choosing or election, and πρόθεσις is purpose or plan (8:28). God's plan works by his own choice, and it "stands", that is, it holds and is carried out.

decisions.choice: the choice rests on God who calls, not on anything done
decisions.reason: Paul stresses that God spoke before the twins were born or had done good or bad. The choice did not depend on works but on God, "the one who calls" (as in 4:17, 8:30).

decisions.choice: the greater, the lesser: the older and the younger
decisions.reason: In Genesis 25:23 the words mean the elder and the younger son, Esau and Jacob.

decisions.choice: what people do
decisions.reason: Readable says "what people do" for "works", as the Romans drafts do throughout.

decisions.choice: Rebecca
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the woman "her" refers to (verse 10).

decisions.choice: God made his choice then
decisions.reason: Readable makes the election in "purpose according to election" a sentence of its own.

records.source: καθὼς γέγραπται· Τὸν Ἰακὼβ ἠγάπησα, τὸν δὲ Ἠσαῦ ἐμίσησα.
records.gloss: Just as it has been written: The Jacob I loved, but the Esau I hated.
pieces: As it is written, "I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated."

L.13: Just as it is written, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated."

R.13: As Scripture says, "I chose to love Jacob, but I rejected Esau."

decisions.choice: Malachi 1:2-3
decisions.reason: Through Malachi, centuries after Jacob and Esau, God answers Israel's doubt of his love by pointing to what happened to their brother nation Edom, descended from Esau (Malachi 1:2-5). In the Hebrew the speaker is named with the divine name. Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament with the names moved to the front.

decisions.choice: loved and hated: chose and did not choose
alternatives: God's feelings of love and hatred toward each
God's active judgment on Esau and Edom
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew way of speaking, "love" and "hate" side by side often mean choosing one and setting the other aside, not feelings: Jacob "loved Rachel more than Leah" and Leah is said to be "hated" (Genesis 29:30-31); compare Luke 14:26 with Matthew 10:37. Here God chose Jacob's line for his covenant and not Esau's. Some take "hated" more strongly, as God's judgment on Edom, which Malachi 1:3-4 goes on to describe.

decisions.choice: the brothers and the peoples descended from them
decisions.reason: Genesis 25:23 and Malachi 1:2-5 speak of the two brothers as the heads of two nations, Israel and Edom. Paul's point is that God's choosing did not depend on birth or works. Whether he is thinking of the choice of individuals for salvation or of the roles of peoples in God's plan is debated; the passage may hold both.

decisions.choice: I chose to love; I rejected
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom as the meaning decision describes it, since "hated" alone suggests a feeling the words do not mean. Literal and Balanced keep "loved" and "hated".

records.source: Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν;
records.gloss: What then will we say?
pieces: What then are we to say?

R.14: So what should we say about this?

decisions.choice: Paul raises an objection to answer it
decisions.reason: Paul uses this question to bring up a conclusion someone might draw from what he has said (as in 3:5, 4:1, 6:1, 7:7, 8:31).

records.heading: Is God unjust?

records.source: μὴ ἀδικία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ;
records.gloss: Not injustice with the God?
pieces: Is there injustice on God's part?

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The question begins with μὴ, which expects a negative answer: "Surely there is no injustice with God?"

decisions.choice: injustice: wrongdoing, failing to be right
decisions.reason: ἀδικία is the opposite of righteousness: if God chose Jacob before either did anything, is God acting unrighteously? Paul asked a similar question in 3:5.

decisions.choice: unfair
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday word for injustice in a choice between two people.

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο·
records.gloss: Not may it be;
pieces: Certainly not!

decisions.choice: the strongest possible denial
decisions.reason: μὴ γένοιτο, "may it not happen", is Paul's strongest way of rejecting a false conclusion (3:4, 3:6, 6:2, 11:1).

decisions.choice: Certainly not! (B); Of course not! (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use ordinary English for an emphatic no, as Galatians does. "God forbid" adds a word for God that the Greek does not have.

records.source: τῷ Μωϋσεῖ γὰρ λέγει· Ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ, καὶ οἰκτιρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτίρω.
records.gloss: To the Moses for he says: I will have mercy on whom ever I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom ever I have compassion.
pieces: For God says to Moses, "I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whomever I show compassion."

L.15: For to Moses {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomever I have compassion."

R.15: God said to Moses, "I will show mercy to anyone I choose. I will be kind to anyone I choose."

decisions.choice: Exodus 33:19
decisions.reason: After Israel made the golden calf, Moses asked to see God's glory. God answered that he would pass by and proclaim his name, and added these words. Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament word for word. The words come just after God has spared Israel in mercy.

decisions.choice: "on whom I have mercy": God alone decides
decisions.reason: Repeating the verb ("I will have mercy on whom I have mercy") is a Hebrew way of saying that the decision is God's own and is not controlled by anything outside him (compare Exodus 3:14).

decisions.choice: the speaker is God
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject; the words are God's in Exodus 33:19.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

decisions.choice: anyone I choose; be kind
decisions.reason: Readable explains the repeated verb as the meaning decision describes it, and uses a simpler word for compassion.

records.source: ἄρα οὖν οὐ τοῦ θέλοντος οὐδὲ τοῦ τρέχοντος ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐλεῶντος θεοῦ.
records.gloss: So then not of the [one] willing nor of the [one] running but of the showing mercy God.
pieces: So it is not a matter of what a person wants or how hard a person strives, but of God, who shows mercy.

L.16: So then [it is] not of the [one] who wills nor of the [one] who runs, but of God who shows mercy.

R.16: So God's choice does not depend on what people want or on how hard they try. It depends on God, who shows mercy.

decisions.choice: "it" is God's choosing and his mercy
decisions.reason: The sentence has no subject. From verses 11-15 it is God's choice to show mercy: it does not come from a person's will or effort.

decisions.choice: running: effort, as of a runner in a race
decisions.reason: Paul often pictures effort as running (1 Corinthians 9:24-26, Galatians 2:2, Philippians 2:16).

decisions.choice: what a person wants; how hard a person strives (B); how hard they try (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "willing" and "running" stand for.

decisions.choice: God's choice
decisions.reason: Readable supplies the subject, as the meaning decision explains it.

records.source: λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ τῷ Φαραὼ ὅτι Εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐξήγειρά σε ὅπως ἐνδείξωμαι ἐν σοὶ τὴν δύναμίν μου, καὶ ὅπως διαγγελῇ τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ.
records.gloss: Says for the Scripture to the Pharaoh that: For this very [thing] I raised up you, so that I might show in you the power of me, and so that might be proclaimed the name of me in all the earth.
pieces: For Scripture says to Pharaoh, "This is the very reason I raised you up: to display {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} power in you, and so that {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name would be made known through the whole earth."

L.17: For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, "For this very [purpose] I raised you up, so that I might show {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} power in you, and so that {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name might be proclaimed in all the earth."

R.17: In Scripture God says to Pharaoh, "This is the very reason I put you where you are: to show {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} power by what I do to you, so that people all over the earth will hear about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: Exodus 9:16
decisions.reason: God says this to Pharaoh through Moses during the plagues, before the hail. Paul's wording is close to the Greek Old Testament, with "raised you up" where it has "kept you".

decisions.choice: raised you up: brought you onto the scene
decisions.reason: ἐξεγείρω can mean to raise up or bring forward. In Exodus 9:16 the Hebrew means "I have let you stand", that is, kept you alive and in power. Paul's word puts the stress on God having brought Pharaoh into his place in history.

decisions.choice: Scripture says: God speaks in Scripture
decisions.reason: In Exodus God speaks these words; Paul says "the Scripture says", as he does in Galatians 3:8.

decisions.choice: my name: God himself, as he makes himself known
decisions.reason: God's name stands for who he is and his fame; the exodus made the God of Israel known among the nations (Exodus 15:14-16, Joshua 2:9-11).

decisions.choice: I put you where you are; will hear about me
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "raised you up" and "my name might be proclaimed" mean, following the meaning decisions.

decisions.choice: God says
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the speaker in Scripture.

records.source: ἄρα οὖν ὃν θέλει ἐλεεῖ, ὃν δὲ θέλει σκληρύνει.
records.gloss: So then whom he wills he has mercy on, and whom he wills he hardens.
pieces: So then God has mercy on whomever {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} chooses, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hardens whomever {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} chooses.

L.18: So then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has mercy on whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wills, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hardens whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wills.

R.18: So God shows mercy to anyone {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} chooses, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} makes stubborn anyone {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} chooses.

decisions.choice: hardens: makes stubborn, unwilling to listen
alternatives: to make someone sinful who was not
decisions.reason: σκληρύνω is to make hard, and so to make a person stubborn against God. In Exodus God says he will harden Pharaoh's heart (4:21, 7:3), and Pharaoh also hardens his own heart (8:15, 8:32). Paul's conclusion draws on both verses 15 and 17.

decisions.choice: God is free in mercy and in hardening
decisions.reason: Paul states the conclusion of verses 15-17 without softening it. The objection in verse 19 shows that he means God's free decision; in 11:7-11 and 11:25-32 he says that Israel's hardening is partial and is not God's last word.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God as the subject.

decisions.choice: makes stubborn
decisions.reason: Readable says what "hardens" means here.

records.source: Ἐρεῖς μοι οὖν· Τί οὖν ἔτι μέμφεται;
records.gloss: You will say to me then: Why then still does he find fault?
pieces: So you will say to me, "Why does God still find fault, then?"

L.19: You will say to me then, "Why then does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} still find fault?"

R.19: Someone will say to me, "If that is true, why does God still blame people?"

decisions.choice: an imagined objector
decisions.reason: Paul answers an objection in the voice of an imagined speaker, as he does in 2:1-5, 3:1-8 and 11:19. The objection follows from verse 18.

decisions.choice: find fault: blame, hold people guilty
decisions.reason: μέμφομαι is to find fault with someone and hold them to blame.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God as the one who blames.

records.heading: The potter and the clay

records.source: τῷ γὰρ βουλήματι αὐτοῦ τίς ἀνθέστηκεν;
records.gloss: For the will of him who has resisted?
pieces: For who can stand against {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} will?

R.19: After all, who can go against what God has decided?

decisions.choice: a rhetorical question: no one has ever resisted
decisions.reason: The perfect tense ἀνθέστηκεν means "who has taken a stand against". The objector means that no one can, so people cannot be blamed.

decisions.choice: his will: his settled purpose
decisions.reason: βούλημα is an intention or decision, here what God has decided to do.

decisions.choice: what God has decided
decisions.reason: Readable names God and says what "his will" means here.

records.source: ὦ ἄνθρωπε, μενοῦνγε σὺ τίς εἶ ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενος τῷ θεῷ;
records.gloss: O man, rather you who are, the [one] answering back to the God?
pieces: But who are you, a mere human being, to answer back to God?

L.20: O {{gender:human|man}}, rather, who are you, the [one] who answers back to God?

R.20: But you are only a human being. Who are you to argue with God?

decisions.choice: O man: a human being, in contrast to God
decisions.reason: ἄνθρωπος here is a human being of either sex; the point is the difference between creature and Creator.

decisions.choice: rather: correcting the objector
decisions.reason: μενοῦνγε turns the question around: rather than calling God to account, who are you?

decisions.choice: answering back: disputing with God
decisions.reason: ἀνταποκρίνομαι is to reply against, to contradict or dispute (compare Job 40:2).

decisions.choice: a mere human being (B); only a human being (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the contrast with God, which the address "O man" carries.

records.source: μὴ ἐρεῖ τὸ πλάσμα τῷ πλάσαντι Τί με ἐποίησας οὕτως;
records.gloss: Not will say the thing formed to the [one] having formed: Why me did you make thus?
pieces: Will what was shaped say to the one who shaped it, "Why did you make me this way?"

L.20: Will the thing formed say to the [one] who formed [it], "Why did you make me like this?"

R.20: A clay pot does not say to the one who made it, "Why did you make me like this?"

decisions.choice: Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9
decisions.reason: Isaiah twice pictures a pot speaking back to the potter who made it, to show how foolish it is for people to question their Maker. Paul uses the wording of Isaiah 29:16 in its Greek form.

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The question begins with μὴ: the thing made has no ground to complain to its maker.

decisions.choice: a clay pot
decisions.reason: Readable names the thing formed from the picture in verse 21, and turns the question into a statement, the answer it expects.

records.source: ἢ οὐκ ἔχει ἐξουσίαν ὁ κεραμεὺς τοῦ πηλοῦ ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ φυράματος ποιῆσαι ὃ μὲν εἰς τιμὴν σκεῦος ὃ δὲ εἰς ἀτιμίαν;
records.gloss: Or not has authority the potter over the clay out of the same lump to make one for honor vessel, and one for dishonor?
pieces: Has the potter no right over the clay? From one and the same lump he may make one pot for honored use and another for common use.

L.21: Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

R.21: A potter has the right to do what he wants with his clay. From the same lump he can make one pot for special use and another for everyday use.

decisions.choice: the potter and the clay in Jeremiah 18:1-6
decisions.reason: At the potter's house God showed Jeremiah that, like clay in the potter's hand, Israel is in God's hand to shape (Jeremiah 18:6). Isaiah uses the same picture (29:16, 45:9, 64:8).

decisions.choice: honor and dishonor: honored use and common use
decisions.reason: The pots differ in use, not in quality: one for special occasions, one for ordinary or menial use, as in 2 Timothy 2:20.

decisions.choice: authority: the right to decide
decisions.reason: ἐξουσία is the right or authority to act; the potter has every right over his clay.

decisions.choice: a question followed by a statement (B); two statements (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced splits the long question; Readable states the answer the question expects (yes).

records.source: εἰ δὲ θέλων ὁ θεὸς ἐνδείξασθαι τὴν ὀργὴν καὶ γνωρίσαι τὸ δυνατὸν αὐτοῦ ἤνεγκεν ἐν πολλῇ μακροθυμίᾳ σκεύη ὀργῆς κατηρτισμένα εἰς ἀπώλειαν, καὶ ἵνα γνωρίσῃ τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ σκεύη ἐλέους, ἃ προητοίμασεν εἰς δόξαν, οὓς καὶ ἐκάλεσεν ἡμᾶς οὐ μόνον ἐξ Ἰουδαίων ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ἐθνῶν ὡς καὶ ἐν τῷ Ὡσηὲ λέγει· Καλέσω τὸν οὐ λαόν μου λαόν μου καὶ τὴν οὐκ ἠγαπημένην ἠγαπημένην·
records.gloss: But if wanting the God to show the wrath and to make known the power of him bore in much patience vessels of wrath having been prepared for destruction, \v 23 and so that he might make known the riches of the glory of him upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory, \v 24 whom also he called, us, not only from Jews but also from Gentiles, \v 25 as also in the Hosea he says: I will call the not people of me people of me, and the not having been loved having been loved;
pieces: What if God, wanting to show {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wrath and to make {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power known, has borne with great patience the vessels of wrath, made ready for destruction?
What if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did this to make known the riches of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory to the vessels of mercy, which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} prepared in advance for glory,
that is, to us, whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has called not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles?
As {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says in Hosea, "Those who were not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people I will call '{{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people,' and her who was not loved I will call 'loved.'"

L.22: But [what] if God, wanting to show the wrath and to make {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power known, bore with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,
L.23: and [did so] in order to make known the riches of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory upon vessels of mercy, which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} prepared beforehand for glory,
L.24: [even] us, whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} also called, not only from [the] Jews but also from [the] Gentiles?
L.25: As {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} also says in Hosea, "I will call [those who were] not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people '{{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people,' and her [who was] not loved 'loved.'"

R.22: Suppose God wanted to show {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger and make {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} power known. Suppose {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has been very patient with people who deserve {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger and are headed for destruction.
R.23: And suppose {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did this to show how great and rich {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory is to the people {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has shown mercy to, people {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} prepared long ago to share {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory. Who could complain about that?
R.24: We are those people. God has called us, and not only from among the Jews, but also from among people who are not Jews.
R.25: This is what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says in the book of Hosea: "I will call those who were not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people '{{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people.' I will call those who were not loved 'loved.'"

decisions.choice: an "if" with no "then": the conclusion is left for the reader
alternatives: a statement of what God has done
decisions.reason: Paul begins "but if God ..." and never finishes the sentence: after the Hosea quotation he moves on. The unstated conclusion is most likely "who are you to object?" (verse 20), or "is God not free to do this?" In context the sentence works as a question: "what if God ...?"

decisions.choice: wanting: either "although he wanted" or "because he wanted"
decisions.reason: The participle θέλων can mean that God bore with them patiently although he wanted to show his wrath (holding it back, as in 2:4), or because he wanted to show it more fully in the end. The first fits Paul's stress on God's patience and on his purpose of mercy in verse 23 and in 11:22-32, but the participle itself allows both.

decisions.choice: prepared for destruction: Paul does not say by whom
decisions.reason: Of the vessels of mercy Paul says "which he prepared beforehand" (verse 23), with God as subject. Of the vessels of wrath he uses a passive or middle perfect, κατηρτισμένα, "made ready", without naming who made them ready. Some read it as God's doing, others as their own (compare 2:4-5, where impenitence stores up wrath).

decisions.choice: vessels: pots, meaning people
decisions.reason: σκεῦος continues the potter's picture from verse 21: people are the pots, made for wrath or for mercy.

decisions.choice: wrath: God's judgment against sin
decisions.reason: As in 1:18 and 2:5, ὀργή is God's settled opposition to evil and his judgment on it, not a fit of temper.

decisions.choice: Hosea 2:23 (2:25 in the Hebrew)
decisions.reason: Hosea's children were named "Not my people" and "Not pitied" as a sign of God's judgment on Israel, and God promised to reverse the names (Hosea 1:6-9, 2:23). Paul quotes freely, with "I will call" and "loved" where the Greek Old Testament has "I will say" and "pitied". He applies to Gentiles a promise first spoken to Israel: God makes his people of those who were not.

decisions.choice: Suppose ... Who could complain about that?
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the unfinished sentence into short "suppose" sentences and states the question the meaning decision takes to be implied.

decisions.choice: anger
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday word for wrath.

decisions.choice: vessels
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "vessels", which ties back to the potter in verse 21; Readable says "people", the meaning of the picture.

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says "people who are not Jews" for "Gentiles", as Romans 1 does.

records.source: καὶ ἔσται ἐν τῷ τόπῳ οὗ ἐρρέθη αὐτοῖς· Οὐ λαός μου ὑμεῖς, ἐκεῖ κληθήσονται υἱοὶ θεοῦ ζῶντος.
records.gloss: And it will be in the place where it was said to them: Not people of me you, there they will be called sons of God living.
pieces: "And in the place where they were told, 'You are not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people,' that is where they will be called {{gender:children|sons}} of the living God."

L.26: "And it will be [that] in the place where it was said to them, 'You [are] not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people,' there they will be called {{gender:children|sons}} of [the] living God."

R.26: "In the same place where they were told, 'You are not {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people,' they will be called {{gender:children|sons}} of the living God."

decisions.choice: Hosea 1:10 (2:1 in the Hebrew)
decisions.reason: Paul joins a second promise from Hosea to the first, word for word as in the Greek Old Testament: the people once disowned will be called children of the living God. In Hosea the place is the land of Israel; Paul applies the promise to Gentiles wherever God calls them (verse 24).

decisions.choice: sons: children of God, women and men
decisions.reason: The phrase speaks of the people as God's family and heirs, as in 8:14-17, where sons and children are used together. It includes women and men alike.

decisions.choice: the living God: the true God, in contrast to idols
decisions.reason: The title marks the God of Israel as the one who lives and gives life, unlike the idols Hosea condemns (Hosea 4:12-13; compare 1 Thessalonians 1:9).

records.source: Ἠσαΐας δὲ κράζει ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ· Ἐὰν ᾖ ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ ὡς ἡ ἄμμος τῆς θαλάσσης, τὸ ὑπόλειμμα σωθήσεται·
records.gloss: Isaiah and cries out on behalf of the Israel: If be the number of the sons of Israel as the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved;
pieces: And Isaiah cries out about Israel: "Though the people of Israel are as many as the grains of sand by the sea, the remnant will be saved."

L.27: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel, "If the number of the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved;"

R.27: Isaiah also called out this message about Israel: "The people of Israel may be as many as the grains of sand on the seashore. But it is the remnant, the ones who are left, who will be saved."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 10:22, with Hosea 1:10
decisions.reason: Isaiah 10:22-23 says that though Israel is as many as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return, for destruction has been decreed. Paul begins with the words of Hosea 1:10, "the number of the sons of Israel", which he has just quoted from (verse 26). The Hebrew of Isaiah has "return", which the Greek Old Testament gives as "will be saved".

decisions.choice: the remnant: both warning and hope
alternatives: only a remnant will be saved (warning only)
a remnant will surely be saved (hope only)
decisions.reason: The words warn that not all Israel, but a remnant, will be saved (verse 6). They also promise that a remnant will surely be saved, as Paul says in 11:5. Paul may mean both; the Greek says "the remnant will be saved", with no word for "only".

decisions.choice: cries out: proclaims aloud, as a prophet
decisions.reason: κράζω is to shout or cry out; here it is a prophet's urgent message.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "the people of Israel" for "the sons of Israel", which means all the Israelites.

decisions.choice: the ones who are left
decisions.reason: Readable explains "remnant".

records.source: λόγον γὰρ συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων ποιήσει κύριος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.
records.gloss: Word for completing and cutting short will do Lord upon the earth.
pieces: "For on the earth the Lord will carry out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sentence, fully and without delay."

L.28: "For [the] Lord will carry out [the] word upon the earth, completing [it] and cutting [it] short."

R.28: "The Lord will do what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has said {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will do on the earth. He will do it completely and quickly."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 10:23
decisions.reason: Paul continues the quotation of Isaiah 10:22-23 in a shortened form of the Greek Old Testament. The Hebrew of 10:23 names God as "the Lord" with the divine name and "of hosts"; Paul's Greek has only κύριος, "Lord".

decisions.choice: a word completed and cut short: a sentence carried out fully and swiftly
alternatives: the Lord will cut his people down to a remnant
the Lord will settle accounts quickly
decisions.reason: λόγος here is God's spoken decision, in Isaiah a sentence of judgment. συντελέω is to bring to completion and συντέμνω to cut short. Together they most likely mean that God will carry it out fully and without delay. Some take "cut short" to mean that God will reduce Israel to a remnant.

decisions.choice: the shorter text
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT follows the oldest manuscripts. Many later manuscripts add words from the Greek of Isaiah 10:22-23: "in righteousness, for a word cut short", giving "he will complete the word and cut it short in righteousness, for the Lord will do a word cut short on the earth". Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: sentence
decisions.reason: Balanced says "sentence" for "word", as the meaning decision explains it.

decisions.choice: do what he has said; completely and quickly
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the meaning decision takes the phrase to mean.

records.source: καὶ καθὼς προείρηκεν Ἠσαΐας· Εἰ μὴ κύριος Σαβαὼθ ἐγκατέλιπεν ἡμῖν σπέρμα, ὡς Σόδομα ἂν ἐγενήθημεν καὶ ὡς Γόμορρα ἂν ὡμοιώθημεν.
records.gloss: And just as has said beforehand Isaiah: If not Lord Sabaoth had left to us seed, as Sodom we would have become and as Gomorrah we would have been made like.
pieces: And as Isaiah said earlier, "If the Lord of hosts had not left us some descendants, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah."

L.29: And just as Isaiah has said beforehand, "If [the] Lord Sabaoth had not left us seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah."

R.29: Isaiah had also said this earlier: "If the Lord who commands the armies of heaven had not left us a few descendants, we would have been wiped out like the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 1:9
decisions.reason: Isaiah describes Judah laid waste by invaders, with Jerusalem left like a hut in a field. Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament word for word. In the Hebrew the title is the divine name followed by the word for armies.

decisions.choice: Sabaoth: armies, God as commander of the heavenly hosts
decisions.reason: Σαβαώθ is a Hebrew word for armies, left untranslated in the Greek, as in James 5:4. The title calls God the ruler of all the powers of heaven.

decisions.choice: seed: a few survivors, from whom the people could grow again
decisions.reason: The Hebrew of Isaiah 1:9 has "a few survivors"; the Greek Old Testament says "seed". A seed is small, but it carries the future, like the remnant of verse 27.

decisions.choice: Sodom and Gomorrah: cities destroyed without survivors
decisions.reason: God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah for their wickedness (Genesis 19:24-25). They became the picture of total destruction (Deuteronomy 29:23, Isaiah 13:19).

decisions.choice: said beforehand: earlier in Isaiah
decisions.reason: προλέγω can mean "foretold" or "said earlier". Isaiah 1:9 comes earlier in the book than 10:22-23, just quoted; the word may also suggest that the prophet spoke ahead of time.

decisions.choice: Sabaoth (L); of hosts (B); who commands the armies of heaven (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew word as the Greek does; Balanced uses the traditional English title; Readable says what it means.

decisions.choice: wiped out like the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah
decisions.reason: Readable says what being "like Sodom" means and joins the two parallel lines.

records.source: Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν;
records.gloss: What then will we say?
pieces: What then are we to say?

R.30: So what should we say about all this?

decisions.choice: Paul draws a conclusion
decisions.reason: As in verse 14, the question introduces the next step. Here it leads to Paul's own conclusion about Gentiles and Israel (verses 30-33).

records.heading: Israel and the stone of stumbling

records.source: ὅτι ἔθνη τὰ μὴ διώκοντα δικαιοσύνην κατέλαβεν δικαιοσύνην, δικαιοσύνην δὲ τὴν ἐκ πίστεως·
records.gloss: That Gentiles, the [ones] not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness, righteousness but the [one] from faith;
pieces: That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have obtained it, the righteousness that comes by faith.

L.30: That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness, a righteousness that [is] from faith;

R.30: We should say this: people who are not Jews were not trying to be right with God. Yet they received righteousness, the righteousness that comes through faith.

decisions.choice: righteousness: being in the right with God
decisions.reason: As in 1:17 and 3:21-22, righteousness here is the right standing with God that he gives to those who believe.

decisions.choice: pursuing and attaining: a chase or a race
decisions.reason: διώκω is to run after, and καταλαμβάνω to catch or seize. Paul pictures a race in which the ones who were not running won the prize (compare Philippians 3:12-14).

decisions.choice: "that" gives the answer to "what then will we say?"
decisions.reason: The clause states the conclusion that the question asked for.

decisions.choice: trying to be right with God
decisions.reason: Readable says what pursuing righteousness means, following the meaning decision.

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says "people who are not Jews" for "Gentiles", as Romans 1 does.

records.source: Ἰσραὴλ δὲ διώκων νόμον δικαιοσύνης εἰς νόμον οὐκ ἔφθασεν.
records.gloss: Israel but pursuing law of righteousness to law not did arrive.
pieces: But Israel, who pursued a law that held out righteousness, did not reach that law.

L.31: But Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not arrive at [that] law.

R.31: But the people of Israel chased after a law that promised righteousness, and they never caught up with that law.

decisions.choice: a law of righteousness: the law of Moses, which held out righteousness
decisions.reason: νόμος here is the law God gave Israel. "Of righteousness" most likely means the law viewed as the way to righteousness, which it promised to those who keep it (10:5, Leviticus 18:5). Some take νόμος here in the general sense of a rule or principle.

decisions.choice: did not reach the law: did not reach what the law aimed at
decisions.reason: Paul keeps the picture of a race: Israel ran after the law but never reached it, that is, never attained the righteousness the law pointed to. Verse 32 says why, and 10:4 says where the law was leading.

decisions.choice: held out righteousness (B); promised righteousness (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "a law of righteousness" means, following the meaning decision.

records.source: διὰ τί;
records.gloss: Because of what?
pieces: Why not?

decisions.choice: the question asks why Israel did not reach it
decisions.reason: The question asks the reason for verse 31: why Israel, who pursued the law, did not reach it.

decisions.choice: Why not? (B); Why did this happen? (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear what the short question asks.

records.source: ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐξ ἔργων· προσέκοψαν τῷ λίθῳ τοῦ προσκόμματος, καθὼς γέγραπται· Ἰδοὺ τίθημι ἐν Σιὼν λίθον προσκόμματος καὶ πέτραν σκανδάλου, καὶ ὁ πιστεύων ἐπ’ αὐτῷ οὐ καταισχυνθήσεται.
records.gloss: Because not from faith but as from works; they stumbled on the stone of the stumbling, \v 33 just as it has been written: Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and the [one] believing on him not will be put to shame.
pieces: Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as though it came by works. They stumbled over the stone that makes people stumble,
as it is written, "See, I am setting in Zion a stone to stumble on, a rock that makes them fall, and whoever believes in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will not be put to shame."

L.32: Because [they pursued it] not from faith but as [if it were] from works. They stumbled over the stone of stumbling,
L.33: just as it is written, "Look, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and the [one] who believes on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will not be put to shame."

R.32: Because they did not seek it by faith. They tried to get it by what they did. So they tripped over the stone that makes people trip.
R.33: As Scripture says, "Look! I am putting a stone in Zion that people will trip over, a rock that will make them fall. But anyone who believes in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will not be put to shame."

decisions.choice: a shortened sentence: "because they pursued it not by faith but as by works"
decisions.reason: The verb is left out and is supplied from verse 31. ὡς, "as", marks works as what they thought the way to it was: they pursued it as if it came from works.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 28:16, with Isaiah 8:14
decisions.reason: Paul joins two passages. Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a tested cornerstone God lays in Zion, and of the one who trusts; Isaiah 8:14 says that God himself (in the Hebrew, named with the divine name) will be a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense for both houses of Israel. Where the Hebrew of 28:16 has "will not be in haste", the Greek Old Testament has "will not be put to shame". Paul quotes the last line again in 10:11, and 1 Peter 2:6-8 joins the same two passages.

decisions.choice: the stone is Christ
decisions.reason: For Paul the stone is the Messiah, a crucified Messiah being a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23); 10:9-11 applies the last line to believing in the Lord Jesus. Some take the stone to be God himself, as in Isaiah 8:14, or the law. The pronoun αὐτῷ can be "him" or "it" (the stone).

decisions.choice: Zion: Jerusalem, where God dwells among his people
decisions.reason: Zion was the hill of the temple in Jerusalem, and so the city and God's people (Isaiah 28:14, Psalm 2:6).

decisions.choice: put to shame: disappointed in one's trust, especially at the judgment
decisions.reason: καταισχύνω is to be shamed, and so to find one's hope let down. Those who believe will not be disgraced when God judges (5:5, 10:11).

decisions.choice: the shorter text
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT follows the oldest manuscripts. Many later manuscripts add "of the law" after "works" in verse 32, and "everyone" before "who believes" in verse 33 (as in 10:11). Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: what they did
decisions.reason: Readable says "what they did" for "works", as the Romans drafts do throughout.

decisions.choice: a stone that makes people stumble; a rock that makes them fall
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid "rock of offense", where "offense" no longer means a cause of stumbling in everyday English.

decisions.choice: him
decisions.reason: The English follows the meaning decision that the stone is Christ, and so writes "him" rather than "it".
